title: One Fate for All, So Eat Your Bread with Joy
summary: The Teacher concludes that the righteous and the wise are in God's hands, yet the same fate, death, comes to everyone. Since the living still have hope and the dead have no share in life under the sun, he urges his reader to eat, drink, wear white, love his wife, and work with all his might. He observes that time and chance happen to all, and he tells the story of a poor wise man who saved a city and was forgotten.
story: Chapter 8 ended with the Teacher unable to comprehend the work of God. Chapter 9 draws out the consequences. If no one knows what lies ahead, and if death comes to all alike, how should a person live? The Teacher's answer is the fullest statement of his call to joy in the whole book: receive life's ordinary gifts wholeheartedly, because they are God's gifts and because the time for enjoying them is short. The chapter then returns to wisdom's value and its limits. Wisdom is better than strength, but it is often ignored. This sets the stage for chapter 10's collection of sayings about wisdom and folly.
historical: The chapter contains no datable events. The story of the besieged city in verses 13 to 15 has no named king or city, and it may be a parable rather than a report. Siege warfare, with ramps built against a city's walls, was well known in the ancient Near East; Assyrian palace reliefs show such ramps, and one was built at Lachish when Sennacherib besieged it in 701 BC. The story's point does not depend on identifying the event. Some readers have compared it with the wise woman of Abel Beth-maacah, who saved her city from Joab's siege by her counsel (2 Samuel 20:14-22), though the Teacher's hero is a man and his story ends differently: no one remembered him.
cultural:
Verses 7 to 9 describe festive life. White garments were worn at celebrations and were practical in a hot climate, while oil on the head was a sign of joy and refreshment (Psalm 23:5; Psalm 104:15). The advice closely resembles a passage in the Old Babylonian version of the Epic of Gilgamesh, in which the alewife Siduri tells the grieving hero that since the gods allotted death to humanity, he should fill his belly, make merry day and night, wear clean clothes, wash his head, cherish the child who holds his hand, and let his wife delight in his embrace. The resemblance is real, but the setting differs. In Gilgamesh the advice is a consolation for the impossibility of escaping death. In Ecclesiastes it is framed by the conviction that God has already approved your works (verse 7) and that life is God's gift (verse 9).

Sheol in verse 10 was the Hebrew name for the realm of the dead, pictured as a shadowy place beneath the earth where the dead continue in a diminished existence without work, planning, knowledge, or wisdom. The Old Testament rarely speaks of anything beyond it until later texts such as Daniel 12:2 speak of resurrection.
literary: The chapter has three parts. Verses 1 to 6 are reflection on the common fate: the same end comes to the righteous and the wicked, the clean and the unclean, the one who sacrifices and the one who does not. The list is built on pairs of opposites to show that no distinction matters to death. Verse 4 is a proverb (a live dog is better than a dead lion), especially pointed because dogs were despised scavengers and lions were symbols of royal power. Verses 7 to 10 are a series of imperatives: go, eat, drink, let your garments be white, enjoy life, do it with all your might. Verses 11 to 18 return to observation, with a proverb about time and chance, an image of fish and birds caught suddenly in a net, and the parable of the poor wise man. The last verse sums up with a double-edged proverb: wisdom is better than weapons of war, but one sinner destroys much good.

outline.t: All are in God's hands, and one fate comes to all
The living have hope; the dead know nothing
Eat, drink, love, and work with all your might
Time and chance happen to all
The poor wise man who saved a city and was forgotten

doctrines.note: The righteous and the wise and their deeds are in God's hands (9:1), even though no one knows what lies ahead. Time and chance happen to all (9:11), but the Teacher does not treat chance as a rival to God; it is how events look from below, to those who cannot see God's purposes.

Bread, wine, clean clothes, marriage, and work are good gifts to be enjoyed with a cheerful heart (9:7-10). The Teacher's call to joy rests on the conviction that God has approved these things and given them as a person's portion.

There is hope for anyone among the living (9:4). Within the limits of Old Testament revelation, the Teacher's hope is modest, the hope of the one still alive to act and enjoy. Later Scripture will speak of a hope that reaches beyond the grave, but the Teacher's honesty about death is part of why that hope, when it comes, is so striking.

words.note: Miqreh, what happens, fate, or chance event. It appears twice in verses 2 and 3: one fate comes to all. The word does not mean an impersonal force called Fate but simply what befalls someone, and in Ecclesiastes it usually refers to death. The Teacher uses it to show that death does not sort people by their virtue.

Sheol, the realm of the dead. In verse 10 it is where the reader is going and where there is no work, planning, knowledge, or wisdom. The Old Testament uses the word for the grave and for the shadowy underworld. Its bleakness here is the reason to act now: whatever you do, do it while you can.

Cheleq, portion. It appears twice: the dead no longer have a portion in anything done under the sun (verse 6), and enjoying life with your wife is your portion in life (verse 9). The word marks the contrast between the two states. The living have a share given by God, and wisdom lies in receiving it.

Et, time. In verse 11 time and chance happen to all, and in verse 12 no one knows his time, meaning the hour of disaster or death. The word links back to the poem of chapter 3. The Teacher now stresses how little humans can control or predict the times that come to them.

christ: The Teacher says that the dead know nothing and have no further reward (9:5). He speaks from within the limits of what had been revealed, and the New Testament answers his observation with an event: Christ has been raised from the dead as the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep (1 Corinthians 15:20). Paul's conclusion to that chapter, that labor in the Lord is not in vain (1 Corinthians 15:58), can be read as a direct reply to the Teacher's fear that death makes all labor futile. The poor wise man who saved a city and was forgotten is not a prophecy of Christ, but many readers have noticed the resemblance: Paul says that Christ, though rich, became poor for our sake (2 Corinthians 8:9), and the one who saved the world was despised and rejected (Isaiah 53:3). The call to eat and drink with joy also finds its fulfillment in the meal Jesus gave his followers, a feast in which death itself is remembered and overcome.

hard.q: Does Ecclesiastes teach that there is no life after death?
hard.a: Verses 5, 6, and 10 say that the dead know nothing, have no reward, and have no work or knowledge in Sheol. Read alone, they seem to deny any afterlife, and some groups have used them to teach that the dead are unconscious until the resurrection. Several points help. First, the Teacher speaks deliberately of life under the sun, the world as seen from within human experience, and he says the dead will never again have a share in all that is done under the sun (verse 6). He is describing their absence from this world, not offering a full account of their state. Second, the Old Testament's revelation about life beyond death is limited and grows over time; clear statements of resurrection come later (Daniel 12:2), and the New Testament grounds hope in Christ's resurrection. Third, the Teacher himself says elsewhere that the spirit returns to God who gave it (12:7) and that God will bring every deed into judgment (12:14), which assumes something beyond the grave. Christians disagree on some details of the intermediate state, but the church's confession is the resurrection of the body, which this chapter's honesty about death makes all the more meaningful.

questions: The Teacher tells us to eat our bread with joy because God has already approved our works. How might believing that change the way you enjoy an ordinary meal or a day's work?
Verse 11 says the race is not always to the swift. Where have you seen skill or effort fail to produce the expected result, and how did you respond?
The poor wise man saved his city but no one remembered him. Does it matter to you whether your good work is remembered? Why or why not?
